probe.format_note: 16:9 landscape, low resolution (736x414). Stereo AAC music bed runs to 35.72 s, then 0.89 s of silence over the end card (mean -18.6 dB, peaks at 0 dB). Beat sync of cuts not measured.

rights_note: found by the owner on Pinterest with a style search (file «code animation motion design.mp4»), given by the owner via Downloads/refrencee on 2026-11-03; origin not stated → plan mode ADAPT, never RECREATE

mode.why: third-party product promo of unknown origin: borrow the motion language and look only, never its shots one by one, its object or UI designs, its copy, its logo or its music (owner note). The reference is a software/app workflow launch (UI); a voiceover package whose topic is not software falls back to REEL with this reading as its motion language.

ignored.why: the closing logo build and end card (paper-plane mark, 'LARK' wordmark, 'www.larksuite.com') are a third-party brand; never reused. Our film ends on the brand's own logo outro.

all English UI copy on the screens ('Project', 'Project Overview', 'Time Table', 'news', 'View on your own', 'Overview', 'Results') and the paper-plane app icon are third-party product content; never reused as text or icons
the avatar portrait tiles on the UI screens are third-party illustrated people; never reused
the music track is third-party audio; never reused (L6 builds sound from the storyboard)

method: ffprobe; ffmpeg contact sheets fps=2, 4x3 (7 sheets, all viewed); scene detect gt(scene,0.3) found one cut (14.16 s); gt(scene,0.12) added soft changes at 12.40, 13.24, 14.20, 15.96, 33.88, 33.96 s (most transitions are continuous camera moves, whips and pushes with motion blur that scene detect does not catch). Dense sheets: fps=10 on 3.4-5.0, 6.0-7.6, 8.4-10.0 s; fps=5 on 12.0-15.2, 23.6-26.8, 29.6-32.8 s (all viewed). silencedetect + volumedetect on the audio. Spans between dense windows are read from the 0.5 s sheets and are accurate to about ±0.25 s. Colours read by eye, not sampled.

shots.shot: medium, hero desktop monitor on a round pedestal, small glossy props around it
shots.camera: slow push-in with a slight orbit to the right; shallow depth of field, out-of-focus foreground torus and glass bubble
shots.moves: UI windows pop out of the screen one after another and stack in depth in front of it (each slides forward and scales up with a soft overshoot, stagger about 0.3 s); a column of small avatar tiles pops in at the screen edge; props float gently
shots.text: none readable (tiny placeholder UI labels only)
shots.transition_out: fast change into the next device world between 1.5 and 2.0 s (not caught by scene detect; read from the 2 fps sheet as a quick colour-wash/whip, about 0.2 s, not verified frame by frame)
shots.palette: sky blue to pale blue gradient, white and light-blue UI, glossy blue pedestal
shots.reusable: yes: interface panels peel off the screen and stack in depth in front of their device; motion only, never the UI design

shots.shot: medium, a tablet floating front-on in the centre, one colour world
shots.moves: large out-of-focus glossy spheres, tori and ribbons drift across the foreground and background at different speeds (strong parallax); UI cards on the tablet shift slightly
shots.transition_out: vertical push about 0.25 s (4.1-4.35 s): the next colour world slides down from the top edge over this one with heavy vertical motion blur and a soft seam; the next device lands in the same screen position
shots.palette: monochrome pink: pale pink to hot pink, white highlights
shots.reusable: yes: one device per monochrome colour world, swapped by a vertical push while the device keeps its place in frame; motion only

shots.moves: settles from the push with a small ease-out; soft blurred shapes float; at about 6.0 s part of the screen turns dark as the next world shows through it
shots.transition_out: push through the screen about 0.4 s (6.2-6.6 s): the camera accelerates (ease-in) into the phone's display, its UI panels fly past the lens with motion blur, and the dark world behind the screen fills the frame
shots.palette: monochrome yellow-orange: butter yellow to tangerine, cream UI
shots.reusable: yes: camera flies through a device screen into the next scene; the screen is the doorway; motion only

shots.moves: the object flies fast with streak lines and drifting particles; the scenery slides past with motion blur
shots.transition_out: light wipe to white about 0.4 s (32.0 s): the background blows out to white while the object keeps flying

visual_language: A glossy 3D product film: devices (monitor, tablet, phones) and the interfaces on them are the heroes, surrounded by clouds of soft glossy symbol-objects (tori, spheres, gears, coins, ribbons, cones, glass bubbles). Medium: full 3D render, no flat illustration and no on-screen headline type; the only words are tiny UI labels. Each section lives in a monochrome colour world (blue, pink, yellow, dark navy, then a bright cobalt-violet-cyan world that carries the second half) and the camera almost never stops: slow push-ins and orbits on the devices, fast fly-throughs and chases between them. Rhythm: 13 readable shots in 32 s (about 2.4 s average), but most changes are continuous camera moves, whips, pushes and light wipes rather than cuts (one hard cut at 14.16 s); a music bed runs under the film, beat sync not measured. Moves are smooth and weighty in the holds (ease-in-out, gentle floating) and fast with motion blur in the transitions (0.2-0.4 s, ease-in into the move, ease-out on landing); UI elements pop in with small overshoots and short staggers. Signature moments: the flashlight beam revealing icons in the dark and then flooding the frame as a wipe; the camera flying through a phone screen into the next world; a paper sheet curling up into a screen; the window exploding into its layers inside a ribbon tunnel; the glass hand tapping and the interface answering; the bookend return to the opening monitor.
look: Real 3D (not flat, not 2.5D): rounded, bevelled devices and soft-touch glossy plastic props with broad soft speculars; frosted translucent glass (the stylised hand, glass slabs, bubbles with refraction); a glossy reflective floor in the low-angle shot; soft diffuse studio light with gentle ambient occlusion and soft contact shading, no hard shadows; strong shallow depth of field with large out-of-focus foreground objects; heavy motion blur on whips and chases; one dark section lit only by a volumetric spotlight cone. Backgrounds are smooth gradient studios and abstract curved surfaces (no real-world setting). Colour: saturated monochrome worlds (sky blue, pink, yellow-orange, navy, cobalt-violet-cyan) with orange/yellow accents.
code_translation: Not code-native (3D render). Per D55 it is built as real 3D in code with three.js: RoundedBox and lathe/tube geometry for devices, pedestal, tori, ribbons (TubeGeometry along curves); MeshPhysicalMaterial with clearcoat for glossy plastic, transmission + roughness for frosted glass (hand, slabs, bubbles), a reflective floor (MeshPhysicalMaterial or reflector); soft key light plus hemisphere/environment fill, soft shadows only; a SpotLight with a volumetric cone mesh (additive, soft-edged) for the dark reveal; depth of field as a bokeh/blur pass; motion blur by frame blending or directional blur on fast moves. UI screens are canvas textures drawn in code with brand colours and shaped Persian text (never split joined letters), mapped onto the device screens; panels that leave the screen are separate thin rounded planes in depth. Colour worlds are large gradient backdrops whose colours come from brand roles. Never flattened into 2D shapes.
continuity: The camera never stops: scenes are joined by camera moves (push, orbit, chase, whip) rather than cuts, so the film reads as one flight.
Fly through a screen: the camera accelerates into a device's display and the next scene is behind it.
Monochrome colour worlds: each section owns one colour; a vertical push swaps world and colour while the hero object keeps its place in frame.
Light as a wipe: a moving light source reveals subjects in the dark, then swings into the lens and floods the frame into the next, brighter scene; a blow-out to white leads into the outro.
One shape becomes another: a flat sheet curls up into a screen; a drawn line folds into a flying object.
Exploded view in motion: an object splits into its layers in depth and reassembles while travelling.
Close foreground passes: an object crossing the lens at full blur hides a change of shot.
Interaction drives change: a stylised glass hand taps and the interface responds (pop, rearrange, scroll), so every state change has a cause on screen.
Build-on: an empty surface is filled element by element (lines draw, blocks pop with short staggers).
Bookend: the film returns to its opening composition, now in a finished state, before the outro.
Burst reveal: a rushing object turns into the hero while small objects explode outward around it.
risks: Third-party product promo of unknown origin (closing brand mark and URL visible): ADAPT only. Never copy the device/UI designs, the paper-plane mark, the glass-hand design, the UI copy, the avatar portraits, the music, or the shot order one by one.

Source is 16:9 landscape; our default is 9:16: compositions must be rebuilt vertically (device centred and larger, symbol objects stacked above and below, chases turned to vertical travel where it reads better), inside the 9:16 safe zone.

The reference has almost no readable on-screen text: our Persian text must be added as its own layer (or as large UI text on the screens) with full hold times and minimum sizes; tiny UI-label scale from the reference is never used for words the viewer must read (readability ranks above the reference).
Fast fly-throughs with heavy blur and dutch angles (r1-s6, r1-s11, r1-s13) cannot carry text; keep them short, between voice lines, or as transitions.
Low source resolution (736x414): fine UI details and exact easing are estimated; spans outside the dense windows are about ±0.25 s.
The 1.5-2.0 s change from the blue to the pink world was not checked frame by frame; L5 should use the vertical push (r1-s2) as the verified world-swap.

The UI mode suits software/app topics; for other voiceover topics, devices and screens are replaced by subjects from the voiceover drawn in the same glossy 3D style (setting comes from the voiceover, never from this footage).

Reference colours (sky blue, pink, yellow-orange, navy, cobalt-violet-cyan, orange accents) map onto brand colour roles as colour worlds; never used as literal hex values; banned brand colours are dropped from the world sequence. Colours were read by eye, not sampled.
Text direction for Persian follows references/rtl-grammar.md (the reference has no text flow to follow).
The reference's music sets a smooth, continuous pace; L6 builds its own sound from the storyboard.
